jess: FYI hitting a pretty nasty hang in the Android SDK when token refresh fires while a coroutine is cancelled. Repro in sample app fairly reliably on emulator.

jess: Logs and short stack:
```text
java.lang.IllegalStateException: request already executed
  at okhttp3.internal.connection.RealCall.execute(RealCall.kt:123)
  at com.redwood.sdk.network.TokenAuthenticator.authenticate(TokenAuthenticator.kt:48)
  at okhttp3.internal.http2.StreamAllocation.findConnection(StreamAllocation.kt:221)
  ...
```

jess: Using okhttp 4.10.0 + retrofit 2.9.0 + coroutines 1.6.4. Authenticator does a synchronous refresh (simple POST to /auth/refresh) and returns a new request. If I cancel the coroutine that kicked off the original call while refresh is in-flight, the app sometimes deadlocks and the request thread never returns. Emulator only reproducible when device is under CPU pressure.

max: @jess I ran into something similar before. TL;DR: Authenticator is synchronous by design and can block OkHttp dispatcher threads — if your refresh ends up re-entering the client or waits on the same dispatcher you can get thread starvation. Two options:
- move refresh logic out of Authenticator into an Interceptor/synchronized token provider that does blocking refresh on a separate small okhttp client
- or make the Authenticator use a dedicated okhttp client with tight callTimeout and its own Dispatcher

max: example pattern that worked for us (Kotlin pseudo):
```kotlin
val refreshClient = okHttpClient.newBuilder()
  .dispatcher(Dispatcher().apply { maxRequests = 4; maxRequestsPerHost = 2 })
  .callTimeout(20, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
  .build()

class TokenAuthenticator : Authenticator {
  override fun authenticate(route: Route?, response: Response): Request? {
    synchronized(tokenLock) {
      val cached = tokenProvider.getCached()
      if (cached != null && response.request.header("Authorization") != "Bearer $cached") {
        return response.request.newBuilder().header("Authorization", "Bearer $cached").build()
      }
      val newToken = tokenProvider.refreshBlocking(refreshClient) // blocking call but on dedicated client
      return if (newToken == null) null else response.request.newBuilder().header("Authorization", "Bearer $newToken").build()
    }
  }
}
```

sara: also: make sure you never execute network calls on the main thread inside authenticate. And set a callTimeout / connectTimeout on that refresh client so cancelled coroutines can't stall forever. For a quick workaround set:
```
okHttpClient.dispatcher.maxRequestsPerHost = 8
okHttpClient.callTimeout = 30s
```

jess: good points. My authenticator was using the main OkHttp client and refreshBlocking() ends up calling the same retrofit instance which uses the same dispatcher — classic deadlock. I'll switch to a dedicated client and add a small dispatcher constraint. Thanks.

max: For SDK parity note — iOS handles this by doing refresh outside of the URLSession auth handler and queuing retry. We should probably match that behavior in Android SDK: intercept -> suspend refresh -> retry. For non-suspend code paths Authenticator with dedicated client is acceptable.

devex-bot: Related issue created: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk/issues/412 (auth-refresh/cancel-hang). Please add repro steps and attach emulator trace.

jess: Will open a PR with a fix in the sample app, add an integration test that cancels the coroutine mid-request and assert no thread hangs. Repro steps I'll add to the issue:
1) run emulator (Pixel 4 API 30)
2) start sample app auth-flow
3) trigger network throttle (10% CPU in emulator) or adb shell to simulate load
4) press back/cancel while request is inflight
5) observe the thread dump / deadlock

sara: :+1: Please also document recommended Authenticator pattern in the SDK docs (devex page) so onboarding teams don't copy the blocking-main-client anti-pattern.

jess: thanks y'all — I'll get the PR in today and ping back here once CI + emulator test pass. :pray:
